questions.prompt: A paper claims its method 'generalises to unseen robots'. Its experiments use one simulated robot with 3 different maps. What is the best assessment?
options: The claim is supported if the average success rate across the maps is high enough.
The claim is supported, because testing on three different maps shows it generalises.
The claim cannot be assessed at all unless the authors also release their code.
The claim is wider than the evidence: one simulated robot on new maps does not test unseen robots.
questions.explanation: Evidence supports only the conditions it tested. New maps test map generalisation, not robot generalisation.

questions.prompt: Baseline success rates over three seeds are 50, 54, 52; the new method gets 55, 57, 56. What is the difference in means (new minus baseline)?
questions.explanation: Means are 52 and 56, so the difference is 4.0.

questions.prompt: For the same data (baseline 50, 54, 52; new 55, 57, 56) compute the standard error of the difference in means using sample variances. Give 2 decimals.
questions.explanation: Sample variances are 4 and 1; SE = sqrt(4/3 + 1/3) = 1.29.

questions.prompt: A paper says 'the gain comes from component C'. Which evidence best supports that claim?
options: The full system beats the baseline on all of the test maps by a clear margin.
A longer and more detailed description of how component C works internally.
A citation to an earlier paper in which component C was already used.
The full system compared with the same system lacking only C, over several seeds.
questions.explanation: A mechanism claim needs a controlled removal (ablation) of that component, repeated enough to see through noise.

questions.prompt: Per-run standard deviation is about 4 points and you want to detect a true difference of 2 points with z = 2. How many runs per method are needed (n >= 2(z*sigma/delta)^2)?
A paper shows a controller working in simulation and claims it is ready for a real robot. List three assumptions the result depends on and how you would check each one.
rubric: Names at least three concrete assumptions (e.g. perfect state estimate, ideal actuation, friction model, fixed initial conditions).
For each, says how it could fail on hardware.
Gives a measurable check for each (noise injection, latency measurement, randomised starts).
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the first pass when reading a paper?
options: To verify every proof and re-derive every equation before reading further.
To list all references that must be read before the next pass begins.
To decide quickly what kind of paper it is and whether it deserves more time.
To reproduce the experiments so the main results can be trusted.
questions.explanation: The first pass (about 5-10 minutes) establishes category, context, correctness impressions, contributions and clarity, and decides whether to continue.

questions.prompt: Write a function (code or pseudocode) that takes a dict of claims, each listing evidence ids, and a dict of evidence, and returns the claims that have no supporting evidence. State one thing it cannot tell you.
rubric: Loops over claims and checks whether any listed evidence id exists in the evidence dict.
Returns the ids with none (not those with some).
Notes it cannot judge the quality, scope or noise of the evidence that exists.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.
